module-11.question: In a method, what does self refer to?
options: The current object the method was called on
The class name as a string
Every Student object in the program at once
The return value of __init__
module-11.explanation: Inside methods, self is the instance you called the method on — for example the specific Student whose summary you want.

module-11.question: What is the difference between a class and an object?
options: A class is the blueprint; an object is one concrete instance made from that blueprint
A class stores data; an object can only store functions
An object is written in the file; a class exists only at runtime
They are two names for the same Student value
module-11.explanation: Student is the class (blueprint). Student("Alex", 92) creates one object with its own name and score.

module-12.question: When is a dataclass usually the better first choice?
options: When the type mainly stores fields and needs little custom setup
Whenever you want the deepest inheritance tree possible
Only when you refuse to print field values
Only for functions that never hold data
module-12.explanation: @dataclass is built for record-style classes — title, points, status — so you skip hand-writing a basic __init__.

module-12.question: Which relationship is the clearest reason to use inheritance?
options: GradedTask is a CourseTask that adds a score field
A report file has many tasks, so Report must inherit from CourseTask
Any two classes that share a print statement should inherit
Inheritance is required before you can use a dictionary
module-12.explanation: Inheritance fits an “is a” relationship. A report that has tasks should usually compose (hold) tasks, not inherit from them.

module-13.question: What do strip() and title() do to the string " ada "?
options: Remove edge spaces, then capitalize it to Ada
Delete all letters and leave only spaces
Convert it to an integer score
Search for digits with a regular expression
module-13.explanation: strip() clears leading/trailing whitespace; title() capitalizes each word — " ada " becomes "Ada".

module-13.question: In this lesson, what does re.search(r"\d", name) check?
options: Whether the name contains at least one digit
Whether the name is exactly three words long
Whether the file path exists on disk
Whether the average score is above 90
module-13.explanation: The pattern \d means a digit. search looks for that pattern anywhere in the string, which is how User42 is flagged.

module-14.question: Why must you check for an empty scores list before computing an average?
options: Dividing by len(scores) when the list is empty causes a ZeroDivisionError
Empty lists automatically average to 100
sum() refuses to run on any list of integers
round() only works when the list is empty
module-14.explanation: average = total / count needs a non-zero count. Guard empty data so the summary skips or reports clearly instead of crashing.

module-14.question: Which set of values best describes a useful score summary?
options: count, total, average, minimum, and maximum
only the average, with no count
only the first score in the list
the class name and the file path
module-14.explanation: Those five numbers let a reader understand both the center (average) and the spread (min/max), plus how much data (count/total) supports the claim.

module-15.question: Why should you convert due and today into date objects before subtracting?
options: Date objects support subtraction and expose a .days count; plain date strings do not
Strings automatically know calendar math in Python
isoformat() deletes the due date so subtraction is unnecessary
strftime always returns the number of days left
module-15.explanation: due - today works on date values and yields a timedelta. Subtracting "2026-06-15" - "2026-05-29" as strings fails.

module-15.question: While learning days-left math, why use a fixed sample today?
options: So the printed day count stays stable and easy to verify across runs
Because date.today() is illegal in Python
Because ISO dates only work with year 2026
Because negative day counts are impossible otherwise
module-15.explanation: A fixed today makes expected output checkable. After the math is clear, you can switch to date.today() for live schedules.

module-16.question: What is the main purpose of comparing expected and actual in a small test?
options: To prove whether the function’s result matches the rule you stated
To replace print() forever with silent programs
To convert syntax errors into dataclasses
To hide logic errors by setting expected = actual
module-16.explanation: A test freezes the expected answer from the rule, runs the function for actual, and shows PASS/FAIL so mismatches are obvious.

module-16.question: Which situation is a logic error rather than a crash?
options: add_points subtracts instead of adds, so the program prints Pass: False
Python refuses to run because a parenthesis is missing
The program crashes with ZeroDivisionError on an empty list
The file name is wrong so python3 cannot open it
module-16.explanation: Logic errors run to completion but return the wrong result. Syntax problems and many runtime exceptions stop the program before you get a quiet wrong answer.
